hook: Fly from the Arctic to the Amazon and the land below changes in a predictable order: bare tundra, dark conifer forest, leafy forest, then grassland or desert, then rainforest. Plants follow climate, and animals follow plants. Two numbers, how warm a place is and how much precipitation it gets, predict most of what you would see.

prereq.q: Which of these is an abiotic factor?
prereq.why: Rainfall is nonliving; the others are living, so biotic.

prereq.q: A community is best described as...
options: all the populations of different species living in one area
the nonliving parts of an area
the place where one species lives
prereq.why: A community is every population living and interacting in one place.

figure.caption: A simplified map of biomes by average yearly temperature and yearly precipitation.

chain.cause: A place has a certain temperature and precipitation pattern
chain.effect: only some kinds of plants can grow there

chain.cause: The plants that grow set the structure (grass, shrubs, conifers, broadleaf trees)
chain.effect: they decide which animals can find food and shelter

chain.cause: Places with similar climates on different continents
chain.effect: end up with similar-looking biomes, even with different species

ideas: A biome is a large region with a typical climate and typical plants, found on several continents.
Temperature and precipitation together decide the biome; a climatograph shows both month by month.
Cold: tundra (with permafrost) and taiga. Temperate: temperate grassland, chaparral, temperate deciduous forest, temperate rainforest. Warm: desert biome, savanna, tropical rainforest.
Going up a mountain changes biomes in roughly the same order as going toward the poles, because it gets colder.

misconception.wrong: A savanna is a desert with some grass, so it gets almost no rain.
misconception.right: A savanna gets a fair amount of rain (often 50 to 130 cm a year), but almost all of it falls in a wet season. A long dry season and fires keep trees scattered.

summary: Terrestrial biomes are set mainly by temperature and precipitation. Tundra and taiga are cold; grassland, chaparral, deciduous forest and temperate rainforest are temperate; desert, savanna and tropical rainforest are warm. A climatograph shows monthly temperature and precipitation, so you can read a biome off it. Savannas are not deserts: they have a wet season and a dry season.
